title: Computational physics
tagline: What to compute when the equation will not solve
summary: Integration of the equations of motion, linear algebra, Monte Carlo methods, fields on a grid, many-particle simulation and the numerical signs of chaos.
overview: Most of the equations in the other courses do not have closed-form solutions. Computational physics is the disciplined replacement of those equations by a finite algorithm whose error you can estimate. The subject is not a programming course. The code is short; the question is whether it computes the thing you think it computes.

Ordinary differential equations come first, because Newtonian mechanics is a system of them: Euler’s method, and why its error forces you on to a Runge–Kutta method, with energy as the diagnostic. Linear algebra is the language of small oscillations, of quantum finite differences and of fitting. Monte Carlo integration and the Metropolis algorithm connect to statistical mechanics. Grids turn Poisson’s equation and the wave equation into matrices. Many-particle simulation adds the cost of the force sum, softening, trees, periodic boundaries, and the measurement of temperature, pressure and structure from a trajectory. The last chapter computes chaos, in the logistic map and the Lorenz system, and then treats data: fitting with $\chi^2$, error propagation, the bootstrap, and the discrete Fourier transform.

Every numerical result in this course should be accompanied by a check against a known limit: energy drift, a halving of the step, or a comparison with an exact solution at a special value of the parameters. A plot is not a check.
outcomes: Integrate a second-order equation of motion and estimate the global error of the method used.
Solve a linear system and a linear eigenvalue problem and know which algorithms are stable.
Estimate an integral and an expectation value by Monte Carlo sampling, with an error bar that accounts for correlation.
Implement a simple Metropolis simulation and state the detailed-balance condition it satisfies.
Discretise Poisson’s equation and the wave equation on a grid and state the stability condition.
Write a molecular-dynamics program with periodic boundaries and measure temperature, virial pressure and the radial distribution function.
Explain the cost of direct force summation and how softening, neighbour lists and the Barnes–Hut tree change it.
Compute a bifurcation diagram and a Lyapunov exponent, and quantify the predictability time of a chaotic system.
Fit a model to data with weighted least squares, judge it by χ², and propagate or bootstrap its uncertainties.
Compute a power spectrum with the fast Fourier transform and recognise aliasing and the Nyquist limit.

history.title: Runge–Kutta
history.detail: Carl Runge published a systematic method for integrating an ordinary differential equation; Martin Kutta generalised it in 1901 to the family of methods that carries both names.

history.title: ENIAC and the Monte Carlo idea
history.detail: Stanislaw Ulam and John von Neumann proposed estimating integrals by random sampling while working on neutron transport. Metropolis and Ulam published the method in 1949.

history.title: The Metropolis algorithm
history.detail: The paper of Metropolis, Rosenbluth, Rosenbluth, Teller and Teller gave a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the Boltzmann distribution.

history.title: The Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou experiment
history.detail: A chain of weakly nonlinear oscillators integrated on the Los Alamos MANIAC failed to share its energy among the modes and returned almost to its initial state, the first great surprise of a computer experiment. Mary Tsingou wrote the program.

history.title: Molecular dynamics
history.detail: Berni Alder and Thomas Wainwright integrated the motion of hard spheres and found a transition between fluid and solid. Aneesur Rahman simulated liquid argon with the Lennard-Jones potential in 1964.

history.title: Lorenz’s equations
history.detail: Edward Lorenz integrated a three-dimensional model of convection and found that trajectories starting close together diverge, the numerical discovery of sensitive dependence.

history.title: The fast Fourier transform
history.detail: Cooley and Tukey published an algorithm for the discrete Fourier transform in O(n log n) operations. Gauss had used the idea; the paper made it a tool.

history.title: Verlet’s integration
history.detail: Loup Verlet published an integration scheme for molecular dynamics that conserves energy well over long runs and is still the default in the field.

history.title: Feigenbaum’s universality
history.detail: Mitchell Feigenbaum published the result that period-doubling cascades in a wide class of maps converge geometrically with the same ratio 4.669…, found in numerical experiments begun in 1975.

history.title: The Barnes–Hut tree
history.detail: Josh Barnes and Piet Hut published a hierarchical algorithm that computes gravitational forces among N bodies in O(N log N) operations by replacing distant groups with their centres of mass.

references.title: Computational Physics
references.note: The book this course follows. It assumes you will write the programs; the physics is in the exercises.

references.title: Computational Physics
references.authors: Nicholas J. Giordano and Hisao Nakanishi
references.note: Second edition. Good on ordinary differential equations and on chaos.

references.title: Numerical Recipes
references.authors: William H. Press, Saul A. Teukolsky, William T. Vetterling and Brian P. Flannery
references.note: Third edition. A reference for the algorithms, not a physics book. Read the warnings as carefully as the code.

references.title: Understanding Molecular Simulation
references.note: Third edition. Molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo for many particles, with the statistical mechanics behind every measured quantity.

references.title: Computer Simulation of Liquids
references.authors: Michael P. Allen and Dominic J. Tildesley
references.note: Second edition. The standard reference for periodic boundaries, neighbour lists, the virial pressure and thermostats.

references.title: Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos
references.note: Second edition. The logistic map, the Lorenz equations and Lyapunov exponents, with the geometry that the numerical chapter assumes.

references.title: An Introduction to Computer Simulation Methods
references.authors: Harvey Gould, Jan Tobochnik and Wolfgang Christian
references.note: Third edition. A wide set of projects, from mechanics to statistical physics.
